name: ZXCT1110W5-7
title: Low-power high-side current monitors, ZXCT1107, ZXCT1109, ZXCT1110
summary: Unipolar high-side current monitors that measure the drop across a shunt in the supply line and return a proportional output current, 4 mA/V, which a single resistor to ground turns into a voltage. They are powered from the sense input itself, need no supply rail, draw about 3 µA, and accept 2.5 V to 36 V of common-mode voltage from -40 °C to 125 °C. The ZXCT1107 and ZXCT1109 are three-pin SOT23 parts with mirrored pinouts; the ZXCT1110 is a five-pin SOT25 with its own ground pin and a tighter, specified offset.

circuits.title: Typical application, ZXCT1107 or ZXCT1109
circuits.description: High-side sensing: RSENSE sits between the supply and the load and the monitor reads the drop across it. The chip draws its own power from S+, so no supply pin is needed; its output current flows into RGAIN to ground and becomes the output voltage. The ZXCT1109 has the same circuit with S+ and S- on swapped pins.

circuits.title: Typical application, ZXCT1110
circuits.description: The ZXCT1110 version of the high-side circuit: the sense resistor carries the load current, S+ and S- read its drop, and RGAIN to ground turns the output current into a voltage. The separate GND pin goes to ground with RGAIN.

circuits.title: Design example, ZXCT1107 or ZXCT1109
circuits.description: Gives 2 V at a 2 A load on a 12 V supply. 50 mΩ puts 100 mV across the inputs at 2 A; 4 mA/V makes that 400 µA, and 5.1 kΩ turns it into about 2 V (5 kΩ would be exact; the 5.1 kΩ preferred value reads 2 % high). With 1 % resistors the total error stays inside ±6 %.

circuits.title: Design example, ZXCT1110
circuits.description: The same 2 V at 2 A target on a smaller shunt. With 4 % allowed for the ZXCT1110, the minimum-sense-voltage equation gives of 37.2 mV (18.6 mΩ at 2 A); 20 mΩ puts 40 mV across the inputs, and RGAIN = 2 / (0.004 × 0.04) = 12.5 kΩ, fitted as 13 kΩ, for ±6 % overall.

circuits.title: Protection and EMC filtering, ZXCT1107
circuits.description: RPROT, 4.7 kΩ in series with S-, holds the input current inside its ±8.5 mA rating when a shorted load puts most of the supply across the sense pins, and with C1 (10 pF across S+ and S-) forms a low-pass filter that knocks down VHF and UHF pickup before it can be rectified inside the chip. C2 is the supply's reservoir capacitor.

circuits.title: Protection and EMC filtering, ZXCT1110
circuits.description: RPROT, 4.7 kΩ in series with S-, holds the input current inside its ±8.5 mA rating when a shorted load puts most of the supply across the sense pins, and with C1 (10 pF across S+ and S-) forms a low-pass filter that knocks down VHF and UHF pickup before it can be rectified inside the chip. C2 is the supply's reservoir capacitor.

circuits.title: 450 V current monitor
circuits.description: Monitors a 200 V to 450 V rail, for example an LED backlight supply. Zener D1 (12 V) fixes the voltage across the chip, biased by R1 (2.2 MΩ) to ground, and the 500 V PNP Q1 carries the output current down to RGAIN and stands off most of the supply. D2 (BAL99) clamps the differential input under overload and so limits the output current to about 3 mA, which keeps the output to a few volts with an RGAIN of a few kΩ. RPROT and C1 are the protection and filter pair. U1 may be a ZXCT1107, ZXCT1109 or ZXCT1110; the ZXCT1110's GND pin joins D1's anode and Q1's base.
notes: A higher RGAIN may need a clamp diode on the output.
R1 is sized to give D1 enough bias current across the supply range.

circuits.title: Pulse response test circuit
circuits.description: The chip's S+ sits at 0 V and its GND pin on a negative supply of -3.7 V or -20 V, decoupled to 0 V. A 50 Ω-terminated pulse generator drives S- through 1 kΩ, with a further 1 kΩ from S- to S+, and the output current develops across 10 kΩ to the negative rail, where an oscilloscope probe reads it.

circuits.title: CMRR test circuit
circuits.description: A +20 V supply feeds the S+ node through 50 Ω, and a 10 mV AC source is coupled onto that node by 2200 µF. The 1 kΩ sense resistor is bypassed by 470 µF and 100 nF, so the AC appears equally on both inputs; 9.1 kΩ plus 200 kΩ from S- to 0 V sets the DC sense current. Channel 1 of a signal analyser watches the input node and channel 2 the output across 2.5 kΩ.

circuits.title: Small signal bandwidth test circuit
circuits.description: S+ sits on a +20 V supply decoupled by 2200 µF and 1 µF. The 1 kΩ sense resistor and 200 kΩ from S- to 0 V set the DC operating point, and a 10 mVpp AC source with a 50 Ω termination is coupled onto S- through 2200 µF, so the AC is differential. Channel 1 reads the S- node and channel 2 the output across 2.5 kΩ.

operation.text: There is no supply pin: the chip takes its power from S+, the positive sense input. The common-mode range is 2.5 V to 36 V and the quiescent current about 3 µA; the S+ current varies with the sense voltage.

All three use the same high-side circuit. The ZXCT1110 (SOT25) adds a GND pin and so has a lower output offset current, which cuts the absolute error. The ZXCT1107 and ZXCT1109 (SOT23, three pins) are mirror images of each other in pin order, to suit tight layouts. On these two the OUT pin is also the substrate, so the rail must be at least 2.5 V above VOUT.

The output is a current, 4 mA per volt of sense voltage. One external resistor, RGAIN, to ground turns it into a voltage for a comparator, an amplifier or an ADC, and its value sets the gain. Above 10 mV of sense voltage the conversion is fully linear.
To avoid extra error the supply must sit at least 1.5 V above VOUT. At VSENSE = 100 mV the margin can shrink to 1.0 V.

A larger shunt cuts the measurement error, especially the random part; a smaller one cuts the voltage lost between supply and load. Pick the sense voltage at the trip current from the error you can accept (the error tables, or ε = ±0.082/VSENSE ± 1.8 % for the ZXCT1110), then add the tolerances of RSENSE and RGAIN to the device error.

A shorted or overloaded load can put a large part of the supply across S+ and S-, and the supply's reservoir capacitor may hold enough charge to destroy the chip before any current limit pulls the supply down. The sense voltage is rated to +0.8 V, but the part survives more as long as the current into S+ and S- is held within ±8.5 mA; a resistor RPROT in series with S- does this without adding noticeable error.

RF picked up on the supply or load wiring can be rectified inside the chip and shift its bias, giving wrong readings. RPROT with a capacitor C1 across S+ and S- makes a low-pass filter that attenuates strongly in the VHF and UHF bands. C1 should be 10 pF to 47 pF, leadless ceramic.

Copper and solder drops on the way to RSENSE give visible error from about 1 A up. Give the shunt the widest copper the current path allows and run the S+ and S- traces only to the resistor's own pads. Place C1, when fitted, right at the S+ and S- pins.
AEC-Q100 Grade 1 qualified automotive variants are offered.
